data.content_ref: inline:SRC_001 asserts a 'shared mechanism' relation between SRC_002 and SRC_004, but the refutation clause is narrowly tailored to an async-routing-phase incompatibility and a program-eval absence, neither of which actually tests whether the mechanism is genuinely shared. The substantive problem asks for a relation that connects the isolated artifact to its neighbourhood; here, naming 'typed-contract enforcement' as a shared mechanism without specifying the overlapping enforcement step (e.g., which program-eval branch both artifacts exercise) reduces the relation to a label. The refutation-if clause does not fire on this deficiency: SRC_004 could require an async routing phase and SRC_002 could still share the same typed-contract label superficially while the underlying eval paths diverge entirely. A genuine shared-mechanism claim must identify the common enforcement operation, not merely assert both use program eval for a forbidden case — every program-eval artifact does that trivially.
